Q: ls -l truncates user name and group name to 8 characters A:

BusyBox ls command truncated username/groupname to 8 characters.

This has been fixed in BusyBox version 1.37.

Q: Get exception localized message A:

Preface:

  • The solution below only works in Windows PowerShell (the legacy, ships-with-Windows, Windows-only edition of PowerShell whose latest and final version is 5.1), because it has been localized to various languages.

    • To see the concrete list of languages available to Windows PowerShell on a given system, run:

      Get-Item $PSHOME\* -Include [a-z][a-z], [a-z][a-z]-*

    • To translate these shorthand culture names, e.g. de-DE, to their full (display) names, run:

      [cultureinfo] 'de-DE'

    • These shorthand culture names correspond do subdirectories in $PSHOME, and inside them you'll find *.dll.mui files that contain the localized text elements for the given culture.

      • Using Windows MUI API functions it should be possible to directly extract localized text elements from these DLLs; however, this would require you to know their (presumably non-public) identifiers; the solution in the next section only shows you how to implicitly retrieve them, by switching PowerShell as a whole to that language and submitting a command that emits the text element of interest.

  • By contrast PowerShell (Core) 7 has not been localized (as of v7.6.x, but that is unlikely to change soon): all its textual resources are English-only; issues related to a potential future localization are being tracked in GitHub issue #19860

To switch Windows PowerShell to a given human language, you must ensure that both:

  • (a) that language is either the install language of your system or has been installed via a language pack (e.g. using the Settings app).

  • (b) [cultureinfo]::CurrentUICulture must reflect the given language, e.g. de-DE for German as spoken in Germany; this can be ensured in one of two ways:

    • Persistently: Use the Settings ap to change the Windows display language;[1] doing so persistently changes the value of [cultureinfo]::CurrentUICulture accordingly.

    • Ad hoc: At the start of a script, set [cultureinfo]::CurrentUICulture explicitly.

      • Caveat: At the interactive prompt, Windows PowerShell unfortunately resets any changes to [cultureinfo]::CurrentUICulture and [cultureinfo]::CurrentCulture after every command execution (fortunately, PowerShell (Core) 7 no longer does that).
        To make a change "stick" in a given interactive Windows PowerShell session / in all future ones via a $PROFILE file, see the workaround in this answer

The following example shows an ad-hoc switch to de-DE as the display language, causing the error message to appear in German:

# NOTE: Windows PowerShell only.
& {

 # Switch the display language to German.
 [cultureinfo]::CurrentUICulture = 'de-DE'

 # Define an advanced script block with a [ValidatePattern()] attribute
 # and pass an argument that fails the validation.
 & { [cmdletbinding()]param([ValidatePattern('^..$')] $param) } 123
  
}

You'll see the following, German error message:

Das Argument für den Parameter "param" kann nicht überprüft werden. Das Argument "123" entspricht nicht dem Muster "^..$". Geben Sie ein Argument an, das
"^..$" entspricht, und führen Sie den Befehl erneut aus.
In Zeile:8 Zeichen:65
+  & { [cmdletbinding()]param([ValidatePattern('^..$')] $param) } 123
+                                                                 ~~~
    + CategoryInfo          : InvalidData: (:) [], ParameterBindingValidationException
    + FullyQualifiedErrorId : ParameterArgumentValidationError

[1] A convenient command for jumping directly to the relevant page in the Settings app is
Start-Process ms-settings:regionformatting
There you can also choose to install additional languages.
